title: "Your First Job"

## [1.8]{.secnum} Run Your First Job {#first-job}

Create a file named `hello.slurm`:

```{.bash filename="hello.slurm"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --output=hello-%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=general
#SBATCH --time=00:02:00
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

echo "Job ID: ${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
echo "Running on: ${SLURMD_NODENAME}"
hostname
date
```

Every batch script has the same shape: the `#!/usr/bin/env bash` line, a block of `#SBATCH` directives that tell Slurm what to reserve, and then ordinary shell commands. The `#SBATCH` lines must come before any real command. Here is what this header asks for:

| Directive | Meaning |
|:----------|:-------------------------------|
| `--job-name=hello` | A label shown in `squeue`. |
| `--output=hello-%j.out` | File for the job's printed output; `%j` is replaced by the job ID, so each run gets its own file. |
| `--partition=general` | Which queue to run in (see [Section 1.6](server.qmd#partitions)). |
| `--time=00:02:00` | Maximum wall-clock time (HH:MM:SS). Slurm stops the job if it runs longer. |
| `--mem=1G` | Total RAM reserved for the job. |
| `--cpus-per-task=1` | How many CPU cores to reserve. |

The lines after the header run on the compute node. Variables such as `$SLURM_JOB_ID` and `$SLURMD_NODENAME` are set by Slurm, so a script can report where and how it ran.

Submit and inspect it:

```bash
sbatch hello.slurm
squeue -u $USER
ls
cat hello-*.out
```

The `*` in `hello-*.out` is a shell *wildcard*: it stands for "any characters here", so `cat hello-*.out` prints whichever `hello-<jobid>.out` file the run created without you having to type the exact job ID.

If you omit `--partition`, the job runs in the default `interactive` partition, which stops jobs after 8 hours. For batch work, set `--partition=general`.

## [1.9]{.secnum} A Complete Example: Run Python from Scratch {#python-from-scratch}

This is the whole workflow end to end to install and run a Python job: install a Python distribution, create an isolated environment with the packages you need, write a small program, and run it as a Slurm job. Every command is included; do it once and the pattern repeats for every project.

### Step 1: Install Miniforge (once per account)

Miniforge is a minimal, free Conda installer that uses the community `conda-forge` channel by default. Install it into your home directory:

```bash
cd ~
curl -L -O https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh -b -p $HOME/miniforge3
$HOME/miniforge3/bin/conda init bash
source ~/.bashrc
```

After this your prompt shows `(base)` and the `conda` command is available. You only do this once.

### Step 2: Create an environment with the packages you need

Make one environment per project so versions never clash. Here we install NumPy and pandas as example dependencies:

```bash
conda create --name my_project python=3.11 numpy pandas
conda activate my_project
python -c "import numpy, pandas; print(numpy.__version__, pandas.__version__)"
```

`conda create` builds a fresh, isolated environment. By listing the packages you want immediately after the environment name (here, `numpy` and `pandas`), Conda will install them alongside a compatible Python version. Next, use `conda activate my_project` to switch your current shell into this new environment. Once active, you can add more packages at any time using `conda install <package>` or `pip install <package>`.

::: {.callout-note title="Activate the environment inside the job, too"}
Activating an environment in your login shell only affects *that* shell. A Slurm job starts in a clean shell that does *not* inherit it, so every job script must run `source ~/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh` and `conda activate my_project` itself before calling `python` (see Step 4 below). Sourcing `~/.bashrc` is not enough: in a job it stops before reaching the Conda setup, because it only runs in full for interactive shells.
:::

### Step 3: Write a small Python program

Save this as `~/slurm-test/analysis.py`:

```{.python filename="analysis.py"}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(size=1000)})
data["y"] = 2 * data["x"] + rng.normal(size=1000)

print("rows:", len(data))
print(data.corr())
data.describe().to_csv("summary.csv")
print("wrote summary.csv")
```

### Step 4: Write the Slurm job script

Save this as `~/slurm-test/run_analysis.slurm`. Notice that it activates the *same* environment before running Python, since a job does not inherit whatever environment is active in your shell:

In the job script below, the `set -euo pipefail` line is a safety net: it tells bash to stop immediately if any command fails (`-e`), if it uses a variable that was never set (`-u`), or if any stage of a pipeline fails (`-o pipefail`). Without it, a job can sail past a broken step and quietly produce a half-finished result.

```{.bash filename="run_analysis.slurm"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=general
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

set -euo pipefail

source ~/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate my_project

cd ~/slurm-test
python analysis.py
```

### Step 5: Submit it and read the result

```bash
cd ~/slurm-test
sbatch run_analysis.slurm     # prints: Submitted batch job 12345
squeue -u $USER               # watch it queue, then run
cat analysis-12345.out        # the printed output (use your own job ID)
cat summary.csv               # the file the script wrote
```

That is the full loop. For any new project you repeat Steps 2–5: a fresh environment, your code, a job script that activates that environment, and `sbatch`.

## [1.10]{.secnum} A Lightweight Alternative: uv Instead of Miniforge {#uv}

Miniforge is not the only way to get Python environments on `naranjito`. **uv** is a free, open-source tool that handles Python installation, environments and PyPI packages. It is one self-contained program in your home directory, needs no admin rights, and is usually much faster than Conda. Each environment is an ordinary folder, by default called `.venv` and kept inside the project folder it belongs to.

Which one should you use?

- **uv** when everything your project needs is a Python package on PyPI: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, JAX, and so on.
- **Miniforge** when you also need software that is not a Python package (R, compilers, GDAL, a CUDA toolkit), or when someone hands you a Conda `environment.yml`.

You can have both installed, and nothing in the Miniforge steps above has to change. The steps below redo the walkthrough with uv. Only Steps 1, 2 and 4 differ; Step 3 (`analysis.py`) and Step 5 (submitting the job) are exactly as above.

### Step 1 (uv): Install uv (once per account)

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source ~/.bashrc
uv --version
```

The installer puts the `uv` program (and its companion `uvx`) in `~/.local/bin` and, if that folder is not on your `PATH` yet, adds it through `~/.bashrc` and `~/.profile`. Unlike Miniforge, it adds no `(base)` environment to your prompt. You only do this once; `uv self update` upgrades uv later.

### Step 2 (uv): Create an environment with the packages you need

Create the environment inside the project folder, here `~/slurm-test`, and install NumPy and pandas as before:

```bash
cd ~/slurm-test
uv venv --python 3.11          # creates the environment in ~/slurm-test/.venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # the uv counterpart of "conda activate"
uv pip install numpy pandas
python -c "import numpy, pandas; print(numpy.__version__, pandas.__version__)"
```

`uv venv` builds a fresh, isolated environment in the folder `.venv`. If Python 3.11 is not available yet, uv downloads it into your home directory on the spot, so there is nothing else to install. `source .venv/bin/activate` switches your shell into the environment (the prompt now starts with `(slurm-test)`), and `deactivate` leaves it. An environment can also live anywhere else: `uv venv ~/venvs/jax_gpu` creates a named one, much like a Conda environment. Add more packages at any time with `uv pip install <package>`, which accepts the same package names and version specifiers as `pip`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Use `uv pip`, not `pip`

A uv environment contains no `pip` of its own. Inside one, `python -m pip` fails, and a plain `pip install` runs the system's `pip` (or Conda's), which either refuses or installs the package somewhere else. Always type `uv pip install`.
:::

### Step 4 (uv): Write the Slurm job script

Save this as `~/slurm-test/run_analysis.slurm` instead of the Conda version. It is the same script, except that one line activating `.venv` replaces the two Conda lines. Activating the environment inside the script means the job runs the same way whatever happens to be active in the shell you submit from:

```{.bash filename="run_analysis.slurm"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --output=analysis-%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=general
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

set -euo pipefail

source ~/slurm-test/.venv/bin/activate

cd ~/slurm-test
python analysis.py
```

Write `analysis.py` (Step 3) and submit the job (Step 5) exactly as above.

::: {.callout-note title="Every job script in this guide works with uv"}
Wherever a job script runs `source ~/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh` and `conda activate <env>`, replace those two lines with the activation script of your uv environment, for example:

```bash
source ~/my_project/.venv/bin/activate
```

It needs neither uv nor Conda at run time, so it behaves the same in every job.
:::
